text: In a quiet corner of Andhra Pradesh, a river has cut a gorge of red rock so dramatic that people call it India's Grand Canyon. But the real Grand Canyon, in Arizona, is about four hundred and forty six kilometres long. The stretch of gorge at Gandikota is about seven. So is the nickname fair? In this video we put the two side by side, at true scale, and you'll see why the small one might still be the better trip this winter.
Gandikota. India's Grand Canyon, at true scale.

Gandikota is a village and a fort in Kadapa district, in the south west of Andhra Pradesh. It sits on the right bank of the Penna river, about fifteen kilometres from the town of Jammalamadugu. Here, the river has to squeeze through a range of red hills called the Erramala, and where it squeezes, it has carved a gorge.

The name tells you the whole story. In Telugu, gandi means gorge, and kota means fort. A gorge fort. For about nine hundred years, people have used this canyon as a wall, and built their walls on top of it.

Picture the gorge in cross section. The river runs at the bottom, squeezed to a channel that sources put at about one hundred to two hundred metres wide. On both sides rise steep red cliffs, often quoted at around three hundred feet, roughly ninety metres. And on the right bank, the fort stands on a hill about one hundred metres above the river. Its builders didn't need a moat. The gorge was the moat.

Now, the true scale. The Grand Canyon runs about two hundred and seventy seven river miles, or four hundred and forty six kilometres. At Gandikota, the Penna winds about seven kilometres between the hills. Let's lay the Grand Canyon on the map, starting at Gandikota and heading east. It crosses all of Andhra Pradesh, reaches the coast of the Bay of Bengal, and keeps going, about two hundred and fifty kilometres out to sea. That's more than sixty Gandikotas, end to end.

Depth is just as lopsided. From rim to river, the Grand Canyon averages about one point six kilometres, and at its deepest it drops about one thousand eight hundred and twenty nine metres. That's more than two Burj Khalifas stacked on top of each other. Gandikota's cliffs, at about ninety metres, would be a small step in comparison. Roughly twenty times shallower.

And width. Rim to rim, the Grand Canyon is about sixteen kilometres across near its most visited viewpoints, and up to twenty nine kilometres in places. Gandikota is one to two hundred metres. But here's the twist. The narrowest point of the Grand Canyon, at Marble Canyon, is only about one hundred and eighty metres wide. So at its tightest, the real Grand Canyon looks a lot like Gandikota.

What about the rock itself? Gandikota's cliffs are made of Gandikota quartzite, part of a great pile of ancient layers that geologists call the Cuddapah Supergroup. It began as sand, which was buried, pressed and cemented until it turned into hard pink and red quartzite. Look closely and you can still see ripple marks and cross bedding, left by moving water before there were any animals on land. These rocks date from the Proterozoic eon, but exactly how old is still debated. The Grand Canyon's oldest rocks are close to two billion years old, yet the canyon itself was carved in only the last five or six million years.

The fort's story starts in eleven twenty three, according to the local record called the Gandikota Kaifiyat, when a chief serving the Kalyani Chalukya kings built a small fort of sand here. Under the Kakatiyas and then the Pemmasani Nayaks, commanders of the Vijayanagara army, it became a huge stone fortress. The Pemmasani family held it for close to three hundred years. Its walls carry around forty bastions, and the gorge guards its western and northern sides.

Then the owners kept changing. After Vijayanagara came the Qutb Shahi sultans of Golconda, whose general Mir Jumla took the fort in sixteen fifty. Then the Mughals, the Nawabs of Kadapa, the Kingdom of Mysore, and finally the British, from seventeen ninety one. Eight different powers in about seven hundred years.

Mir Jumla left his mark. He built the Jama Masjid, the mosque with two tall minarets that still stands inside the walls, and he set up cannon foundries. Around that time, the French gem merchant Jean Baptiste Tavernier came here to meet him, and wrote about it in his travels. Why would a gem dealer come to a canyon fort? Historical accounts say diamonds were mined in this region.

Inside the walls today, you can walk through all of it. The Madhavaraya temple, with a great hall of thirty six pillars. The Raghunatha temple, built by the Pemmasani chiefs. The old granary, its vaulted roof held up by two rows of twelve massive pillars. The mosque, a small Charminar, and a pond called Kathula Koneru, the pond of swords. Then you step out to the edge, and the canyon drops away beneath you.

And Gandikota is changing fast. In August twenty twenty five, Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu laid the foundation stone for a tourism project of about seventy eight crore rupees here. By December, reports said the plans include a tent city, a ropeway and a glass walkway. In January twenty twenty six, the Gandikota festival ran for three days, with helicopter rides over the gorge. Several of these projects are still plans, so check what is actually open before you go.

So why go? One. Sunrise and sunset light up the red quartzite, and the river bends right below the viewpoint. Two. It's a canyon and a nine hundred year old fort in one place, and you can walk from a temple to the cliff edge in minutes. Three. It's quiet, for now. The Grand Canyon had about four point four million visitors in twenty twenty five. Four. It's an easy add on to other sights in the region, such as the Belum Caves, often described as among the longest caves in India.

Getting there. The nearest town is Jammalamadugu, about fifteen kilometres away. Kadapa is roughly eighty kilometres, and has the nearest airport. The closest railway stations are Muddanuru, about twenty six kilometres, and Yerraguntla, about forty seven. Bengaluru is around three hundred kilometres away by road, and Hyderabad close to four hundred. The best time to visit is October to February, when the days are pleasant, which makes right now the season.

One honest warning. The cliffs are sheer drops, so stay well back from the edge, especially for that perfect photo. The summer is very hot, and the river can run low. And the ruins are fragile. Don't climb on the old walls, and take your rubbish back with you.

So, is Gandikota India's Grand Canyon? At true scale, the real one is more than sixty times longer and about twenty times deeper. But Gandikota has something the Grand Canyon doesn't: a nine hundred year old fortress sitting right on the edge. Which would you rather see first, the real Grand Canyon or India's?
